headline: Full Moon Torque Puts Bass Back on the Wire at The Race
subhead: Current rebuilt like we said it would, and the stripers came back with it — plus the first real bonito signs are stacking up off Fishers Island.
body_markdown:
Tuesday, 3:40 a.m., east side of The Race. I'm up to my thighs on the rocks below the lighthouse throwing a jointed Gibbs Danny into water that's finally moving with authority again, and on the fourth cast something grabs it like it means business. Forty inches, maybe forty-one, hooked outside the mouth and buried into the current before I could get tight. Took me into the rip twice trying to spool me before I walked her up on the rocks. That's the fish that tells you the moon did its job.

We flagged this one — said the rips would rebuild toward the full moon and the striper and bluefish bite on bait pushed through them would sharpen up noticeably once current strengthened, and that's exactly what happened. The Race is running back in the 4-to-5 knot range on the big swings now, Plum Gut right behind it, and the bass that scattered and sulked during the neap lull are back on the current edges where they belong. This isn't subtle fishing. You're not picking through structure looking for stragglers — you're finding the seam where the moving water meets the slack, and the fish are stacked right on that line waiting for bait to get squeezed through.

The pattern that's working: fish the last two hours of the ebb and first hour of the flood at The Race, working bucktails — 2 to 3 ounces depending on how hard it's ripping — tipped with a white curl-tail or a chunk of fresh bunker, dropped off the edge of the reef structure on the west side and bounced down current. Let it sink clean, don't rush it, then work it back with a slow lift-drop through the seam. Bass have been running mostly mid-20s to low-30s inches with a handful of overslot fish mixed in on the dawn bite — nothing like the 40-plus I stuck Tuesday, but that's the kind of water that produces one big fish out of every dozen decent ones if you put your time in.

Bluefish are the other half of this story and they're not messing around. Jumbo blues, 8 to 12 pounds, are busting bunker pods hard in Fishers Island Sound and right through Plum Gut on the tide changes. Topwater poppers and metal — Deadly Dicks, Ava jigs in the 3/4 to 1-ounce range — are getting hit the second they land when the blues are up and slashing. If you see the birds working tight and nervous water, don't wait, get the boat on it, that window closes fast once the blues push the bait down.

Water's holding in a spot that's actually working in our favor out here. New London's reading right around 70 degrees, cooler than the western Sound, which is keeping the bass comfortable enough to stay active through more of the daylight hours than you'd expect for the second week of August — not an all-day bite, but the dawn and dusk windows are stretching a little longer than they were three weeks ago. Keep an eye on that gradient. If the eastern water holds steady in the high 60s to low 70s while the rest of the Sound keeps warming, this end stays the better play right through Labor Day.

Fluke are the dependable piece right now, and the Niantic fleet is proving the call we made last week — that fishery is basically neap-proof and it's carrying the zone through any current lull. Boats working 38 feet of water off Niantic Bay are still punching limits with white Gulp Swimming Mullets on half-ounce bucktails, dragged slow on the drift over the mixed bottom there. A few doormats in the 6-to-7 pound class have come out of that stretch this week. If the rip bite goes quiet on you for a tide, that's where I'd put the boat.

Porgies are stacked up on the reef structure between Plum Gut and Fishers Island — bloodworms and clam on standard porgy rigs in 25 to 40 feet is still automatic if you're anchored up right on the rock piles. Not glamorous but it fills a cooler while you wait for the tide to turn back in your favor for bass.

Now the one I'm watching hardest — bonito. Water's sitting in that low-to-mid 70s window that historically gets this corridor moving first in the region, and The Race and Plum Gut are usually among the earliest spots to see them stack up when the temp's right. Nothing solid on the deck yet that I'd call confirmed, but the conditions are lining up. I'd have small Deadly Dicks and Albie Snax rigged and ready on a second rod this week just in case the first push shows on the surface — those things materialize fast and disappear just as quick.

Look-ahead: current stays strong through the weekend as we ride down off full moon, so I'd keep hammering the rip edges early and late. By midweek the swings ease back toward standard range — that's when I'd lean harder on Niantic for the sure thing and keep working dawn patrol at the Gut for whatever's still stacked on the seams.
